content.overview: Pre-use checks help technicians establish whether equipment is in its expected controlled state before operation. Learners practice comparing actual condition to readiness criteria, preserving out-of-service status, performing only assigned operator corrections, and escalating faults without turning an inspection into unauthorized troubleshooting.

vocabulary.definition: A defined operator-level inspection performed before use to confirm obvious readiness and safety conditions.
A condition that must be met before an asset is used for the assigned task.
The normal or expected asset condition established by the equipment instructions, SOP, previous controlled status or known operating range.
A controlled status indicating equipment should not be used until the authorized evaluation or release process is complete.

sections.title: Compare the asset to its expected state
sections.body: A useful pre-use check compares actual condition with defined readiness criteria: correct asset identity, current status, cleanliness, visible damage, leaks, hoses/connections, guards/covers, indicators and other asset-specific points. The operator is looking for meaningful change or failed criteria, not trying to perform a full maintenance diagnosis.

sections.title: Status controls matter
sections.body: An out-of-service tag, open maintenance ticket, unresolved prior-shift fault or other controlled restriction remains part of the readiness decision even when the asset looks normal. Technicians do not remove or ignore controlled status simply because the schedule needs the equipment.

sections.title: Inspection does not expand repair authority
sections.body: A missing guard, damaged cord, abnormal leak or failed protective feature can make the asset unready. Finding the defect does not authorize the technician to bypass the safeguard, open protected equipment or perform servicing beyond the operator procedure.

workedExamples: A leaking irrigation connection is handled only through the approved operator response or maintenance escalation.
A missing guard prevents use even if the operator believes careful technique would avoid contact.
An out-of-service tag from the prior shift remains attached even though the equipment powers on; the technician preserves the status and verifies authorized release before use.
A permitted external indicator is outside its readiness range, so the technician records the reading and follows the defined fault path rather than opening the controller enclosure.
commonMistakes: Skipping checks because equipment worked on the previous shift.
Treating 'powers on' as proof that every readiness criterion passes.
Ignoring an open fault or out-of-service status because the equipment looks normal.
Using an improvised repair in place of an authorized maintenance decision.
Turning a pre-use inspection into deeper troubleshooting not assigned to the operator.
content.practicalApplication: Perform a simulated pre-use inspection using an asset packet with prior-shift status, visible conditions, indicators and one planted authorization trap. Classify each finding as ready, approved routine correction, out-of-service/escalation or emergency hazard, and document the evidence supporting the final readiness state.
content.summary: Technicians establish equipment readiness by comparing the actual asset to defined criteria and controlled status. A failed check is a reason to control and escalate the asset, not permission to improvise a repair.

blocks.title: Pre-use checks protect safety and process reliability
blocks.body: A readiness check is not a full maintenance inspection. It is the defined operator review performed before use to catch obvious conditions that make an asset unsafe, unavailable, dirty, incorrectly configured or unreliable for the assigned task.

items.title: Confirm asset identity
items.body: Verify the exact equipment and that it is the asset assigned for the work.

items.title: Check controlled status
items.body: Look for out-of-service tags, open faults, maintenance notes, holds or prior-shift conditions that affect use.

items.title: Compare accessible condition to baseline
items.body: Inspect the assigned external points for cleanliness, visible damage, leaks, hoses/connections, guards/covers, obstructions and other specified criteria.

items.title: Review permitted indicators
items.body: Check readings, alarms, displays or readiness indicators explicitly included in the operator procedure.

items.title: Classify the finding
items.body: Decide whether the asset is ready, needs an approved routine correction, must remain out of service/escalated, or presents an emergency hazard.

items.title: Document final status
items.body: Record what was observed, what permitted action was taken and why the asset was released, held or escalated.

blocks.alt: Diagram separating routine operator care explicitly assigned by equipment and site procedures from servicing that may involve guards, hazardous motion, protected electrical components, powered disassembly, pressure, stored energy, or other hazards requiring the employer-defined authorized role.
blocks.caption: A failed readiness check does not authorize the technician to cross from inspection into servicing.

blocks.title: Readiness finding classification
rows: Asset matches assignment and all specified checks pass
Operate according to the current work instruction
Minor condition with a routine correction explicitly assigned to the operator
Complete the defined correction, verify readiness and record if required
Missing guard, damaged power component, unresolved leak or failed safety criterion
Do not use; preserve status and refer under procedure
Prior out-of-service tag or unresolved open fault
Do not assume visual normality equals clearance; verify authorized release

blocks.title: The guard is missing but the task is behind schedule
blocks.setting: A powered piece of equipment passes its normal indicator check, but a required guard is missing. A coworker says careful hand placement makes it safe enough for one short run.
blocks.prompt: What is the correct Technician I response?
options: Run it once at reduced speed
Do not use the asset; follow the out-of-service/escalation process for the failed readiness criterion
Replace the guard with a temporary improvised cover
blocks.answer: Do not use the asset; follow the out-of-service/escalation process for the failed readiness criterion.
blocks.feedback: A failed protective feature is not corrected by careful technique, extra PPE or an improvised substitute unless a controlled authorized process specifically provides for that action.

blocks.title: The equipment looks normal but remains tagged
blocks.setting: A pump is clean, shows normal external indicators and starts during the permitted status check, but an out-of-service tag from the prior shift remains attached and no release record is available.
options: The fact that the pump starts
The controlled status remains unresolved until the authorized release process confirms it can return to service
Whether the current shift is busy
blocks.answer: The controlled status remains unresolved until the authorized release process confirms it can return to service.
blocks.feedback: Visual condition and startup do not erase controlled status. The technician preserves the restriction until the authorized process releases the asset.

blocks.title: Pre-use readiness record
blocks.description: The record should capture the asset and actual findings rather than a generic 'checked' statement.

fields.label: Prior controlled status
fields.value: Available, tagged, open fault, maintenance note or other status

fields.label: Assigned inspection points
fields.value: Asset-specific readiness criteria from the current procedure

fields.label: Observed condition
fields.value: What was actually seen or read

fields.label: Operator correction
fields.value: Only routine action explicitly allowed by the procedure, if any

fields.label: Final readiness
fields.value: Ready, out of service, escalated or emergency response

fields.label: Notification / ticket
fields.value: Required person, role or maintenance/deviation record

blocks.title: Perform a simulated pre-use inspection
blocks.instructions: Inspect a mock equipment packet containing asset images, status tags, readings and an operator checklist. Classify every finding without performing unauthorized repair work.
prompts: Verify asset identity and prior status.
Identify each readiness criterion that passes or fails.
Separate routine operator corrections from out-of-service conditions.
Identify the finding that crosses into maintenance or hazardous-energy servicing.
Explain why a normal-looking asset can still be unavailable if controlled status is unresolved.
Write the final readiness status and escalation note.

blocks.title: Remediation cue
blocks.body: If your readiness decision depends only on 'it turns on,' 'it looks fine,' or 'we need it today,' go back to the controlled status and asset-specific readiness criteria. Readiness is evidence-based, not schedule-based.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Pre-use competence means finding problems before use, respecting controlled equipment status and staying inside the operator boundary. A failed check is a reason to control the asset—not a license to improvise a repair.
